title: Root wounds facilitate the uptake of microplastics in crop plants

paper_content.abstract: Microplastics can be absorbed by plant roots and enter the food chain. Throughout the plant life cycle, roots frequently encounter various physical injuries. However, whether these prevalent injuries serve as critical pathways for microplastics entry into plants remains unknown. Here we demonstrate that both shallowly wounded roots (injuries limited to cortex) and unwounded roots exhibit effective resistance to the penetration of microplastics. In contrast, deep wounds (injuries extending to the stele) in roots provide a rapid pathway for microplastics to enter crops such as taro (Colocasia esculenta) and maize (Zea mays). Microplastics are rapidly transported upward via wound-exposed xylem vessels in both vermiculite and soil culture conditions. When 20% of the roots were subjected to deep wounds and exposed to vermiculite containing 50 mg kg−1 of polystyrene microplastics, the accumulation levels in taro corms reached 161.1 ± 26.4 (1 μm) and 135.6 ± 24.9 (5 μm) items g−1, while in maize stems reached 503.4 ± 147.4 (1 μm) and 222.3 ± 63.8 (5 μm) items g−1. Our findings provide substantial evidence that root wounds facilitate the uptake, translocation, and accumulation of microplastics in crops, underscoring the urgent need for proper farming practices to prevent root injuries and enhance food safety.
paper_content.introduction:
Microplastics (MPs, with size < 5 mm)1,2 are ubiquitous in marine and terrestrial ecosystems3,4. The global stock of MPs in agricultural soils is estimated to reach 1.5 to 6.6 million tons5. In China, the median MPs concentrations in the topsoil layer (0–15 cm) reach 79.81 mg kg−1.6 MPs can alter soil physicochemical and biological properties7,8, posing potential threats to soil health and even ecosystem multifunctionality9,10. A meta-analysis shows that MPs pollution decreases overall soil health index by 10.2%, with reduced soil bacteria diversity but increased emissions of greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, and N2O), particularly at high doses (>1%) and smaller sizes (<40 μm)11. A growing body of evidence demonstrates that MPs induce a range of adverse effects in plants, including oxidative stress, suppression of root elongation, and impaired nutrient uptake8,12. At environmentally relevant concentrations, MPs of various polymer types have been shown to reduce biomass in multiple crop species, such as lettuce, wheat, maize, and rice13. Among the various mechanisms by which MPs affect plants, the potential for MPs to penetrate roots and translocate to edible parts warrants particular attention8,14. This concern arises from the fact that plants serve as primary producers and the main source of food and forage, representing a significant pathway for human intake of MPs15.

Generally, plant roots can resist the penetration of particles such as MPs due to the dense structure of their intact cell walls16-18. However, research has also demonstrated that MPs can enter plant roots and leaves through different uptake mechanisms such as endocytosis, apoplastic transport, crack entry, and stomatal entry14. One very interesting pathway is the crack-entry mode, i.e., cracks can form at sites of lateral root emergence, providing a transport way for MPs (0.2 and 2 μm) to invade the stele19. Consequently, the structural integrity of roots is essential for preventing the intrusion of MPs. However, wounds or ruptures in the roots caused by underground herbivores or mechanical injuries may also create entry sites for MPs.

Root injury occurs commonly throughout plant life cycle20. During crop cultivation, practices such as inter-tillage, transplanting, root-pruning, weeding, and fertilization are effective for enhancing yield but also result in root trauma21-23. In addition, below-ground herbivores24 and extreme weather events25,26 can also inflict root damage. Due to the loss of barriers, root wounds are an infection site for many soil pathogens27. It is speculated that wounds also provide a shortcut for MPs into the roots19,28, but direct evidence is still lacking. Considering the wide occurrence of root injury, there is an urgent need to confirm whether MPs can enter roots via a wound-entry mode and the underlying mechanisms.

In this study, mechanical wounding is inflicted on roots of four plant species, including taro (Colocasia esculenta), maize (Zea mays), mung bean (Vigna radiata), and wheat (Triticum aestivum). The plants are cultivated in either vermiculite or soil substrates with root systems exposed to 50 mg kg−1 of diverse MPs, which comprise soil-persistent polymer types functionalized with fluorescent tags, including microspheres—polystyrene (PS), polylactic acid (PLA), and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) at diameters of 1 μm, 1.5 μm, and 5 μm—alongside fragments of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polyethylene (PE) exhibiting a size distribution of 0.5–5 μm. Our aims are (1) to investigate whether varying levels of mechanical wounding can increase root uptake of MPs, (2) to unveil whether MPs absorbed by wounded roots enter the edible parts and the associated translocation and accumulation mechanisms, and (3) to quantify the content of MP particles in corms/stems by developing a straightforward and reliable MPs quantification method. Among these four crops, taro is a tuber crop with an edible portion that is directly attached to the root, making it more susceptible to MPs contamination. In contrast, maize, wheat, and mung bean are key representative crops in the forage, grain, and legume categories, respectively. The results will provide direct and universal evidence for the uptake of MPs due to root injury and offer theoretical support for implementing rational farming practices to reduce MPs contamination in agricultural products.
paper_content.results:
Intact plant root could resist the penetration of MPs
The vascular bundles in plant roots were directly connected to those in corms/stems (Fig. 1a). In the case of unwound (UW) taro and maize plants grown in vermiculite, it was observed that 1 μm and 5 μm PS microspheres (PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm) were predominantly attached to the surfaces of the roots and root hairs after 15 days of exposure (Fig. 1c-f). Notably, none of these PS-MPs could be detected either inside the endodermis or in the xylem vessels.

Following 30 days of exposure, minimal changes were observed in the attachment and penetration of PS-MPs to UW roots. No PS-MPs were observed in the vascular tissues of roots, stems/corms, or petioles (Supplementary Fig. S1).

Wounds increased adsorption and absorption of MPs by roots
The adsorption of a large quantity of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm at the wound surface of shallow-wound (SW) taro (Fig. 2a,b) and maize (Fig. 3a,d) roots were observed after only 1 day of exposure in vermiculite. However, these MPs were unable to penetrate the remaining cortical tissues and endodermis, and were thus blocked from reaching the root vascular tissues (Supplementary Fig. S2,S3).

In longitudinal sections of deep-wound (DWI) roots of taro plants, a significant accumulation of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm was observed adhering to the wound surface after 1 day of exposure (Fig. 2c,e). These MPs demonstrated movement upward within the xylem vessels, progressing over 5 cm in distance (Fig. 2d,f). This movement was evident from the beaded arrangement of PS-MPs, with some lodged within the spiral walls of the vessels. Subsequent to 2 days of exposure, numerous PS-MPs were evident within the lumen of xylem vessels at the base of DW roots (Fig. 4a,e). Among these, some PS-MPs were dispersed (Fig. 4a), while some others were clumped and adhered to the inner wall of the vessels (Fig. 2d and Fig. 4e). In addition, after two days of exposure under soil cultivation, both fragmented PVC-MPs and PE-MPs, ranging from 0.5 to 5 μm in size, were found to have entered the xylem vessels at the root bases (Supplementary Fig. S4).

Following a 2-day exposure period in vermiculite, SW treatment demonstrated significant enhancements in the adsorption of PS-MPs to the wound tissue of taro root, with increases of 253.1% for PS-MPs1μm and 572.5% for PS-MPs5μm. However, this treatment did not result in a notable increase in absorption(Fig. 2g, Source Data). In contrast, DW treatment resulted in adsorption increases of 114.6% for PS-MPs1μm and 545.9% for PS-MPs5μm by the wound tissue. The average absorption levels of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm in DW roots reached 695 (±107) μg g−1 and 766 (±135) μg g−1, respectively. There were no significant changes in both adsorption and absorption when the exposure time increased to 5 days (Fig. 2g, Source Data). The absorption of PS-MPs5μm was undetectable in the UW roots, whereas absorption of approximately 15–28 μg g−1 for PS-MPs1μm was observed in UW and SW roots. We contend that this phenomenon should not be characterized as genuine absorption. Instead, it appears to result from a limited number of PS-MPs1μm that are trapped in the interstitial spaces of the root epidermis. As a consequence, these MPs cannot be eluted through sonication. This observation also aligned with the findings presented in Fig. 1c, which illustrates that PS-MPs1μm were tightly bound to epidermal cells. Furthermore, the patterns observed in maize roots treated with SW (Fig. 3) and DW (Fig. 5a,d) closely resembled those seen in taro.

DW treatment induced MPs accumulation in edible parts
Quantifying the amount of MPs absorbed by plants is currently challenging. In this study, we have developed a quantitative method for assessing the presence of fluorescently labeled MPs using serial sections (See Methods). After a 30-day exposure period in vermiculite, no PS-MPs were detected in the corms and petioles of the SW taro plants (Supplementary Fig. S3b,c,e,f). Furthermore, the percentage of vascular bundles containing PS-MPs was assessed in the transverse sections of corms after DW treatment, where 15.0% (PS-MPs1μm) and 18.4% (PS-MPs5μm) of the vascular bundles were identified (Fig. 4b,f,i). These vascular bundles were in close proximity to the DW root attachment sites (Supplementary Fig. S5). It is worth noting that in the corms of the DW taro plants, the abundance of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm was 161.1 (±26.4) and 135.6 (±24.9) items g−1, respectively (Fig. 4j). However, these PS-MPs did not migrate into the petioles and leaves (Fig. 4c,d,g,h). Additionally, soil-derived PVC-MPs and PE-MPs also accumulated in the vascular bundles of the corms (Supplementary Fig. S6a,b), indicating that the wound-entry mode is polymer type- and shape- independent.

In DW maize plants, PS-MPs were also observed in the vascular bundles of the stems (Fig. 5b,c,e). The abundance of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm in the second internode reached 503.4 (±147.4) and 222.3 (±63.8) items g-1 (Fig. 5f), respectively. In parallel, 1.5 μm PLA microspheres (Fig. 6a), 5 μm PMMA microspheres (Fig. 6b), and fragmented PVC-MPs (Supplementary Fig. S6c) were also detected in maize stems. These findings suggest that DW provides a direct and rapid pathway for MPs to enter the edible parts of crops.
paper_content.methods:
Preparation of MPs
This study employed multiple types of MPs to represent the predominant polymer types detected in soil6,50. Polystyrene (PS), polylactic acid (PLA), and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) MPs were commercial microspheres, fluorescently labeled with Rhodamine 6G for orange-red fluorescence. Based on their nominal sizes, they were designated as PS-MPs1μm, PS-MPs5μm, PLA-MPs1.5μm, and PMMA-MPs5μm, respectively. Among them, PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm were the primary types used in this study due to their consistent sizes and spherical shapes, which make them easy to identify under a microscope. This clarity supports the tracking of their transport pathways within plants and the quantification of their accumulation in edible parts. Additionally, to investigate whether the role of root wounds in facilitating the uptake of MPs is independent of polymer types and shapes, polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polyethylene (PE) MPs were prepared by mechanical grinding into fragments. These MPs were then sieved to achieve a size distribution concentrated within 0.5–5 μm and labeled with Nile red for fluorescence, named PVC-MPs and PE-MPs, respectively. The fluorescence properties under red (Ex=525 nm, Em=600-680 nm) and yellow (Ex=490 nm, Em=560-580 nm) channels and actual size distributions of all the above MPs were illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S9.

Stability of fluorescently labeled MP particles
Both in vitro and in vivo experiments were conducted to assess the potential leakage of fluorescent dyes from MPs. In vitro, the size of fluorescent particles in the leachate from culture substrates was analyzed after 30 days of exposure using fluorescence microscopy (Supplementary Fig. S10). In substrates containing 1 μm and 5 μm PS microspheres, it was assumed that the substrate particles remained uncontaminated if only the corresponding size of fluorescent microspheres is present, without any other sizes or shapes. Subsequently, these leachates were filtered through a 3000 Da ultrafiltration centrifuge tube, and the fluorescence intensity of the filtrate was measured using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (F96pro, Lengguang Technology) to determine the presence of any leaked fluorescent substances in the culture solution. Finally, the filtrates were collected for growing new plants, and after 15 days of growth, the root sections were observed using a fluorescence microscope to confirm that the leachate from the substrate did not stain the plant tissues (Supplementary Fig. S11).

In vivo, approximately 1 ng of PS-MPs was injected into the roots using a capillary. The plants were grown in vermiculite that did not contain MPs. After 30 days, sections and fluorescence microscopy were done near the injection site to detect the shape, size, and location of the fluorescence signal (Supplementary Fig. S12). If only fluorescent microspheres of the corresponding sizes were observed in the roots injected with PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm, respectively, and no fluorescent particles of other sizes or diffuse fluorescent signals were observed, it was assumed that there was no significant leakage of MPs in the plant.

Plant materials and growth conditions
Taro (Colocasia esculenta), maize (Zea mays), mung bean (Vigna radiata), and wheat (Triticum aestivum) were selected as the experimental materials. For taro, the terminal buds of the corms were excised, sterilized with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution, and then inoculated into culture flasks containing 1/2 MS medium supplemented with 1% agar for propagation. This process ensured that all experimental materials originated from a single mother plant. Once the seedlings developed 4 to 5 leaves, they were transplanted into 0.6 L nursery pots (one seedling per pot) and cultivated for an additional month. The seeds of maize, mung bean, and wheat were surface-sterilized by soaking them in a 1% sodium hypochlorite solution for 10 minutes, after which they were sown in 0.3 L nursery pots (one seed per pot) and grown for 3 weeks. All pots were filled with sterilized vermiculite and initially irrigated with a 1/2 Hoagland’s nutrient solution. Subsequently, they received irrigation with a 1/10 Hoagland’s nutrient solution every 3 to 7 days, depending on water consumption. All plants were grown in a greenhouse under controlled conditions: temperature of 28 ± 2 ℃, a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, light intensity of 60 μmol m−2 s−1, and relative humidity of 75 ± 5%.

Root wounding and MPs exposure
Plants with uniform growth were deliberately selected for MPs exposure. Before exposure, their roots were carefully washed to remove the peripheral vermiculite. Under a stereomicroscope, a shallow wound (SW) or a deep wound (DW) was created in the selected root using a sterile razor blade. These wounds were positioned in the center of the root: approximately 15 cm from the corm for taro plants and 10 cm from the stem for maize, mung bean, and wheat plants. The wounding treatment was applied to the taproot of the mung bean plant and to about 20% of the adventitious roots of the taro, maize, and wheat plants. SW involved the removal of the epidermis and a portion of the cortical tissue without injuring the inner vascular bundles, resulting in wounds approximately 6 mm in length and 0.3 mm in depth. DW entailed severing the root and exposing the inner vascular tissue (Fig. 1b). Plants that were not wounded were denoted as UW.

MP exposure treatments were conducted using either vermiculite or soil as the growth medium. The vermiculite had a particle size distribution of 0.5–2 mm. Soil samples were collected from the surface layer (0–20 cm) of an agricultural field in Jinan, Shandong Province, China (36.67°N, 117.06°E) during the summer of 2024, prior to sowing. The field operates under a winter wheat-summer maize rotation system. The soil texture was classified as sandy loam and was sieved through a 2-mm mesh, with its physical and chemical properties detailed in Supplementary Table S1. To prevent the invasion of harmful microorganisms and maintain stable wound conditions, both vermiculite and soil were sterilized. Due to the lack of data on the abundance and mass concentrations of MPs < 5 µm in real agricultural soils, the concentration of MPs was designed by comprehensively referencing the survey that the environmental concentrations of MPs in top soils of China’s agricultural fields can reach 1.59 to 816.57 mg kg−1 (median 79.81 mg kg−1)6, and previous studies19,51. MPs of various polymer types and shapes were added to sterilized vermiculite/soil to achieve a final concentration of 50 mg kg−1, with moisture maintained at 60% of the water holding capacity (WHC), followed by incubation for over two weeks. This mass-based concentration corresponds to approximately 9.1×1010 particles kg−1 for PS-MPs1μm and about 7.3×108 particles kg−1 for PS-MPs5μm.

Roots were buried in vermiculite/soil with or without MPs amendment. For taro, 0.6 L pots were used, each filled with approximately 0.36 kg of vermiculite or 0.72 kg of soil; for maize, mung bean and wheat, 0.3 L pots were adopted, with each pot loaded with about 0.18 kg of vermiculite or 0.36 kg of soil. Both vermiculite and soil were weighed at 60% of their WHC. After pot filling, all plants were irrigated with 1/10-strength Hoagland’s solution, followed by subsequent irrigation at 3–7 days intervals according to the water consumption. This irrigation regime allowed vermiculite/soil moisture to cycle between 50% and 100% of the WHC, simulating field irrigation and precipitation patterns. The exposure period varied from 1 to 30 days. Each treatment group included 7 biological replicates.

Observation of MPs in plant tissues
Following exposure, plants were rinsed with distilled water and then divided into root, corm/stem, and leaf segments. These segments were then immersed in a 4% paraformaldehyde fixative (w:v, in 0.1 M PBS, pH=7.3) for 12 hours at room temperature. Subsequently, all samples were washed with distilled water and sliced to a thickness of 100 μm using a sledge microtome. For taro plants, longitudinal sections were obtained from wound sites of SW and DW roots as well as from corm-root attachment zones, while transverse sections were collected from the root base (near the corm), mid-petiole, and mid-leaf regions. For maize, mung bean, and wheat plants, transverse sections were obtained from the root base (adjacent to the stem) and the mid-stem region. All the aforementioned sections were stained using berberine-aniline blue to reveal the xylem vessels and the exodermis and endodermis of the roots. The sections were observed in bright field, red fluorescence (Ex=525nm, Em=600–680nm), yellow fluorescence (Ex=490nm, Em=560–580nm), or blue fluorescence (Ex=365nm, Em=460–500nm) channels. The red and yellow fluorescence channels were employed to identify MPs. The parallel observation of these channels can eliminate the interference of autofluorescence of plant tissues, thus accurately pinpointing the distribution of MPs. The blue fluorescence channel was utilized to identify lignified cell walls.

Quantification of adsorption and absorption of MPs by roots
The adsorption and absorption of MPs in roots were determined using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (F96pro, Lengguang Technology, China) with a modified method.52,53 Specifically, gradient solutions of PS-MPs1μm and PS-MPs5μm were prepared, and their fluorescence intensities (FI) were measured (Ex=465 nm, Em=580 nm) and plotted as a standard curve. Subsequently, the exposed roots underwent gentle rinsing with distilled water. For UW roots, 5 mm segments were collected at the middle of the root; for SW and DW roots, 5 mm segments were collected at the wounded site. Ten root segments were bulked for each sample and weighed. The root segments were then immersed in distilled water (containing 0.1% Tween-20) and subjected to ultrasonic washing three times (30 seconds each) to elute the surface-adsorbed MPs, and the eluates were combined. The washed root segments were homogenized by adding 0.5 mL of distilled water (containing 0.1% Tween-20). The homogenate was filtered through a 1200-mesh sieve, and the residue underwent ultrasonic cleaning with distilled water (containing 0.1% Tween) five times, followed by mixing the filtrates. Finally, the adsorption and absorption of MPs were calculated based on the FI of the eluate and filtrate (minus the background FI of the unexposed sample) and divided by the weight of the root segments, respectively. The unit of measurement is μg g−1, representing the weight (μg) of PS-MPs that can be adsorbed or absorbed per gram of root (fresh weight).

Quantitative analysis of MP particles in taro corms and maize stems
In this study, a quantitative method was developed to quantify MP particles in plant samples. This method is suitable for fluorescently labeled MPs and offers the advantages of accuracy, speed, and cost-effectiveness. Specifically, taro corms and the second internode of maize stems from DW+PS-MPs1μm and DW+PS-MPs5μm groups were collected and thoroughly cleaned using distilled water and a brush. The second internode of the maize stem was chosen for analysis, as the first internode—derived from the mesocotyl—is generally subterranean, whereas the second and higher internodes are situated above ground. The weight of each taro corm was measured at 2804.3 ± 288.2 mg, while the weight of each maize second internode was 196.7 ± 32.6 mg. These plant samples were immersed in 4% paraformaldehyde fixative for 96 hours. Subsequently, taro corms were sectioned into about 50 consecutive sections, each with a thickness of 200 µm (Supplementary Fig. S8), while maize stems were sectioned into around 60 consecutive sections measuring 50 µm in thickness. The number of PS-MPs in each section was observed and recorded under a microscope using the red and yellow fluorescence channels. The MPs content was calculated based on the total number of microspheres in all consecutive sections and the weight of each plant sample, expressed in terms of items g−1 (fresh weight).

Statistical analysis
The microscopic observations were conducted utilizing 7 biological replicates, while quantitative determinations were based on a minimum of 3 biological replicates. Data organization and graphical representation were performed using Microsoft Excel 2021 and Origin software. Significance analyses were carried out using SPSS v21 software. Two-tailed Student's t test was employed to compare independent samples of two groups, and one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s test was used to compare independent samples of three or more groups, with a significance level of P-value < 0.05.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
General Comments:
This paper describes a study focused on evaluating how varying levels of mechanical wounding can increase root uptake of microplastics (MPs), unveiling whether MPs absorbed by wounded roots enter the edible parts, determining associated translocation and accumulation mechanisms, and to quantify the content of polystyrene (PS) particles in corms/stems by developing a straightforward and reliable MPs quantification method. Four crops used for the study encompassed a wide range of crop types: taro (tuber), maize (forage crop), wheat (grain crop), and mung bean (legume crop). The study was conducted to provide theoretical support for the primary mechanisms of MPs uptake by plants and to implement rational farming practices to reduce MPs contamination in agricultural products. The manuscript is well-written; the study was carefully designed and well-conducted. Methodologies are innovative. The authors used a vermiculite growth medium (soil-less) for the study. Therefore, if the authors can explain how this can be extended to soil-based cultivation (Discussion section), it will enhance the value of the study findings and clarify the implications for agriculture. The following are some specific suggestions and comments.
Specific comments and suggestions:
Abstract:
Lines 28-29 “Further quantitative analysis revealed that after 30 days of 28 exposure,” please provide details on the amount of microplastics exposed to plants.
Lines 32-33: The conclusion that needs to be emphasized is that the effect of root wounds can enhance microplastic uptake and translocation. The study was conducted in a soilless culture system, which differs substantially from real-world soil-based agricultural conditions. Therefore, the results are most likely not directly generalizable to all food crops grown in microplastic-contaminated soil. As mentioned under general comments, this needs to be addressed. How can soil organic matter, dissolved C, and properties of MPs influence their movement in soil and uptake by crop plants?
Line 34 is missing the heading “Introduction.”
Methods
Lines 64, 90, 309, 569, etc. are contradictory. A bit confusing here, which type of MPs were used for this study: polyethylene (PS) microplastics, polystyrene (PS) particles, or both? Clearly indicate which type of microplastics were used in this study. Clearly state the reasons for specifically selecting these microplastics PS, polylactic acid (PLA), and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) for the study. Also, in Methods, please define PLA (line 315) and PMMA (line 316).
Discussion
It is worth noting that the authors quantified microplastic abundance in the medium as the number of particles per milligram of microplastic weight used in the current study. While it is clear that 50 mg of microplastics per kilogram of media was used in the experiment, the quantification of microplastics in plant tissues was reported based on the number of particles absorbed by the plant. This raises concerns about the feasibility of achieving such high uptake levels under natural soil-based conditions. Specifically, the results state that over 200 microplastic particles were absorbed per gram of root fresh weight within just 24–48 hours. This raises questions, such as how much water the plant absorbed during that period and whether it could realistically carry such a high microplastic load into the root tissues. This also raises the question of whether MPs in that growing medium are freely moving with water. This is also why one may not be able to extend these findings directly to plant growth in soils.
To accurately assess uptake efficiency and to interpret the environmental relevance of these findings, it is essential to provide quantitative data on the actual amount of microplastics taken up by the plant relative to the total amount applied. This information would not only clarify the exposure-uptake relationship but also significantly improve the applicability of the results to real-world scenarios and future studies examining microplastic behavior in soil-plant systems.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study investigated the uptake of polystyrene microspheres with 1 micron and 5 micron in diameters by taro, maize, mung bean, and wheat as influenced by root wounds in a laboratory experiments. The study observed that root wounds serve as significant entry points for the uptake of polystyrene microspheres and deeper wounds extending to the stele had much greater effects, as the polystyrene microspheres were transported upward via the xylem. This study provided indisputable evidence supporting the important role of root wounds on the entry of microplastics into plants. A few points that would require more clarifications from the authors. First, polystyrene is only one type of plastics used or released in agricultural systems. How could the uniform polystyrene microspheres differ from microplastics in agricultural soils that may be degraded plastic fragments? Second, plant growth in vermiculite was used. How could the condition differ in real soil? Considering the possible attachment of polystyrene microspheres to soil aggregates, how could you interpret your results in the context of crops growing in real soils? What was the water content in vermiculite? Was it fully saturated or unsaturated? Would you think that your experimental conditions would overestimate the uptake of polystyrene microspheres? Third, plant roots may be naturally wounded due to root penetration and growth in real soils. Could you explain more what kind of soils or soil conditions that may lead to more root wounding? What kind of agricultural practices could reduce root wounding? Finally, results and discussion should be combined so that discussion was specific to certain results and the paper can be more concise. Some specific comments are below:
Line 25, “invasion” indicates the active role of plastic microspheres in its movement, which seems unlikely. Suggest to use another word throughout the manuscript.
Line 35-45, this section needs more specifics. At what levels microplastics caused those effects?
Line 62-65, here you should concisely explain how these crops were grown and how exposure of polystyrene microspheres occurred.
Line 337-347, how were the plants grown? Were they grown in a greenhouse or in a growth chamber? What were the growth conditions (e.g., photoperiods, temperature, and relative humidity)? Was the vermiculite fully saturated or unsaturated? Could it represent agricultural soils? If not, how could one interpret the study results in the context of actual cropping systems? Were the plants grown in nursery pots? If so, how many plants in each pots? How many replicates per treatments?
Line 354-356, more description on the plant root wounding is needed. How did you quantify the level of wounding following your wounding treatment?

Response: Thank you very much for your valuable time spent reviewing our manuscript and for your positive feedback on our work. Following your constructive suggestions, we have made comprehensive and meticulous modifications to the manuscript. These revisions have significantly enhanced the clarity of the presentation and the articulation of the research findings' value. In line with your comments, we have added exposure experiments under soil cultivation conditions. These experiments yielded results consistent with those obtained under vermiculite culture (Figures R1.1-R1.3). We have included these data in the revised manuscript (Lines 121-123, 195-197, Line 200-203, Fig. S4,S6). The detailed procedure involved adding fragmented PVC-MPs and PE-MPs, which were produced through a grinding process, into sterilized sandy loam. These MPs had a size distribution of 0.5–5 μm and were fluorescently labeled with Nile red (Figure R1.1). The results indicated that these fragmented MPs were absorbed by deep wounded (DW) roots (Figure R1.2) and entered the corms of taro and the stems of maize (Figure R1.3). These data suggests that the "wound-entry" mode identified in this study can be applied to soil cultivation conditions. Additionally, we have included a discussion on the influence of various factors in farmland soil on the absorption of MPs by wounded roots (Line 312-323).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Thank you for your responses to our questions. Although authors responded to questions, we still have concerns related to whether this study over-predicted and oversimplified how the microplastic (MP) uptake in a realistic, field-based scenario. While we recognize that authors have included some background information to justify that root injuries are common, we remain concerned about several key points:
1. Incorrect interpretation of results in the cited paper. We noted that the paper cited in this study — Wang et al. (2024), Depth distribution of nano- and microplastics and their contribution to carbon storage in Chinese agricultural soils) Specifically considers both nano- and microplastics (NMPs, defined as ≤5 mm) in Chinese farmland soils. Importantly, this means that all plastic particles smaller than 5 mm were included in their analysis when calculating the average soil concentration range. As a result, the reported values in that study represent a broad size spectrum of plastic particles, rather than focusing solely on smaller microplastics (e.g., <150 µm or the size used in the current study (1-5µm)) that are most likely to interact with plants. This distinction is critical, since including the complete ≤5 mm size range may lead to higher reported average concentrations (weight basis 50 mg kg-1) compared to studies that restrict their analysis to smaller size fractions.
2. The amount of MPs applied to the potting mixture
The concentrations used in this experimental setup appear to exceed typical field conditions. For comparison:
• Büks & Kaupenjohann (2020) conducted a comprehensive review of published studies on agricultural and horticultural sites that were exposed to sewage sludge and mulching film application. They found that the common field concentrations were <13,000 items/kg and 4.5 mg/kg soil. These values may be regarded as more realistic upper bounds for experimental simulations.
Büks, F., & Kaupenjohann, M. (2020). Global concentrations of microplastics in soils – a review. SOIL, 6, 649-662.
https://doi.org/10.5194/soil-6-649-2020:
• Lwanga et al. (2023) reported mean soil microplastic concentrations in agricultural fields with plastic mulch ranging from ~128.7 ± 320 MPs/g soil (LDPE mulch) to ~224.8 ± 488 MPs/g soil (PAC mulch), for particles in the 50–150 µm size range. These values represent realistic field scenarios where MPs are present due to specific agricultural practices.
Lwanga, E. H., Van Roshum, I., Munhoz, D. R., Meng, K., Rezaei, M., Goossens, D., Bijsterbosch, J., Alexandre, N., Oosterwijk, J., Krol, M., Peters, P., Geissen, V., & Ritsema, C. (2023). Microplastic appraisal of soil, water, ditch sediment and airborne dust: The case of agricultural systems. Environmental Pollution, 316, 120513.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2022.120513
3. The fraction of MPs absorbed by plants
Another concern relates to the reported bioconcentration factor. For example, maize with mechanically damaged (deep-wounded) roots, the fraction absorbed has been estimated at approximately 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ (503/ 2.9×108 particles of PS-MPs 5μm). This raises a question about the significance of such uptake in real field systems, especially considering the much lower concentrations typically present in soils (complex and heterogeneous both in terms of composition and pore structure) compared to the amounts applied here that used homogeneous potting mixtures. Again, please justify your approach.
4. The severity and frequency of root wounding in field crops
Finally, it is essential to address the occurrence of severe (deep) root wounding events in typical field-grown maize or other crops. Severe mechanical damage to roots, as simulated in some experimental studies, may not reflect the natural frequency of such events under standard agronomic conditions for the crops studied here. This strongly influences the likelihood of MPs entering plants in the field and should be carefully discussed when extrapolating greenhouse or pot experiments to real agricultural systems. Additionally, it is important to consider whether the common agricultural practice of using plastic mulch for maize and similar field crops should also be regarded as a significant concern.
Although we agree that deeply wounded roots can act as one of the major absorption pathways based on the study results, we remain deeply concerned about the generalization and applicability of these findings to real-world agricultural conditions. Further, although the authors attempted to prove that this entry is possible using a soil (thank you for including those results), it didn’t provide quantitative results for the MP uptake by soil-based plants. It would help clarify how soil transports MPs to plants differently, through the soil and wounded roots (i.e., MPs alone, potentially enter with soil particles?). As the main work presented here is still non-soil-based, please explain the novelty of the current study compared to the existing studies, such as https://www.nature.com/articles/s41893-020-0567-9

Response: Both of these questions are about the environmental concentrations of soil MPs, so we have decided to address them together. Indeed, we had carefully investigated the environmental concentrations of MPs in soils before designing the current study. We chose 50 mg/kg to represent a real soil contamination level of MPs for the following reasons.
1.1 Regarding the concentration of MPs in soil.
(1) Although numerous studies have investigated the occurrence of MPs in soils, most of them determined the abundance of MPs based on particle counts (the counts of particles per kg soil). Only a few studies determined the mass concentrations of soil MPs (Wang et al., 2024; Büks & Kaupenjohann, 2020). In the review by Büks & Kaupenjohann (2020), the authors conclude that “the majority of the prospected agricultural and horticultural sites were exposed to sewage sludge and mulching film application and showed concentrations of <13,000 items/kg dry soil and 4.5 mg/kg dry soil.” However, this review only analyzed 23 studies of soil MP concentrations published before August 2020. The methodologies for the separation and quantification of soil MPs are significantly underdeveloped. For example, in this review, “Vollertsen and Hansen (2017) also estimated mass concentrations of 5.8 mg/kg (min – 0.0 mg/kg; max – 16.5 mg/kg) after sludge application and 12.0 mg/kg (min – 0.1 mg/kg; max – 224.3 mg/kg) by use of a shape-to-mass model…. Due to issues with the analysis, the author suggested that the data should be viewed as preliminary results.”
Differently, the paper by Wang et al. (2024) that was cited in our study used a more accurate method, Thermal Desorption/Pyrolysis Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (TD/Py-GC–MS), to directly quantify the mass of MPs in environmental samples. This method has been proven an effective method for direct quantification of MPs mass concentration in environmental samples with complex matrices (Luo et al., 2023; Dierkes et al., 2019). Using this method, Wang et al. (2024) found that the mass concentrations of MPs varied ranging from 1.59 to 816.57 mg/kg dry weight (dw) in the topsoil (0–15 cm), with a median value of 79.81 mg/kg. In a soil sample from Guandong, China, the mass concentration of MPs can reach 1167 mg/kg (Wang et al., 2024). Dierkes et al. (2019) used a pressurized liquid extraction (PLE) in combination with Pyr-GC-MS for the extraction and quantification of PE, PP and PS from soil samples, and found that the mass concentrations PE, PS, and PP MPs in roadside soil reached up to 850 ± 70 mg/kg, 40 ± 5 mg/kg, and 57 ± 5 mg/kg, respectively, and PE mass concentration reached 2800 ± 200 mg/kg in a potting soil bought from in a local store in Koblenz, Germany. Thus, the mass concentrations of MPs reported by Wang et al. (2024) may be more accurate than those estimated by Büks & Kaupenjohann (2020).
(2) We thank your recommended reference Lwanga et al. (2023) that “reported mean soil microplastic concentrations in agricultural fields with plastic mulch ranging from ~128.7 ± 320 MPs/g soil (LDPE mulch) to ~224.8 ± 488 MPs/g soil (PAC mulch), for particles in the 50–150 µm size range.” In this study, the soil samples were collected from the farms of Netherlands. Please note the unit is “MPs/g”. In other words, the concentrations reached ~128,700 (± 320,000) and ~224,800 (± 488,000) items per kg soil, respectively. These values are really high！ Assuming that these MPs exist in spherical form with a diameter of 100 µm, and given that the density of mulch film is generally 0.92 g/cm³, it can be calculated that the mass of 224,800 LDPE MPs is about 108.23 mg (Table R1, middle column). Thus, the MP mass concentration in soil would be 108.23 mg/kg. This is higher than the concentration used in our present study. Furthermore, the study by Lwanga et al. (2023) also pointed out that “The highest content was found in soils exposed to plastic mulch, with the highest content per field reaching 1109 MPs/g of soil” and “The highest microplastic content measured in soils with compost application was 890.2 MPs/g of soil.” This indicates that the mass concentration in heavily contaminated plots could reach 500 mg/kg (Table R1, right column). Certainly, the particle morphology of MPs in natural soil is frequently irregular. While the calculated mass may exhibit certain deviations, the order of magnitude should remain fundamentally consistent.

(3) Another reason is that we should consider the heterogeneous distribution of soil MPs.
The distribution of MPs in soils in the horizontal space is often not uniform but heterogeneous (Rillig et al., 2017; Sun Q., et al., 2022), i.e., MPs are present in one soil microsite (patch) but absent in its horizontally adjacent soil microsites or MPs are present in adjacent microsites with different concentrations. For instance, long-term plastic film mulching and random disposal of plastics may create soil patches with high concentration of MPs. Sewage sludge application, wastewater irrigation, human tillage, soil biota activity, atmospheric deposition and wind- or water-mediated movement may redistribute MPs in soils and create horizontal soil patches with different concentrations of MPs (Zhang et al., 2022). One example is that tillage may cause plastic film residues to gather together, creating plastic hotspots. The content of MPs around the plastic film residues (e.g., plastisphere) may reach a high level. Therefore, in some certain soil microsites, the content of MPs may be very high.
(4) In addition, the long-term application and accumulation effects may lead to continuous increase of soil MPs concentrations. Agricultural plastic film is one of the main sources of MPs in farmland soil (Qi et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022). Conventional plastics are very difficult to degrade, thus leading to accumulation of MPs in soil. A previous studies have confirmed that the abundance of MPs in the farmland continuously covered with mulch film increased with the increase of mulch film covering time (Huang et al., 2020). In addition, in the soil environment, even biodegradable plastics generally have a low degradation rate, leading to the formation of a large quantity of MPs during degradation (Liao and Chen, 2021). Because biodegradable mulching films are generally not recovered after plant harvest, they are likely to accumulate unevenly in the soil and ultimately become hotspots of soil MPs. Fertilization is another pathway of MPs into soil. A prediction shows that, in 50 and 100 years from now, soils treated with fertilizers are expected to reach microplastic concentrations of 168.9 mg/kg (95% CI: 60.32-473.09) and 1159 mg/kg (95% CI: 200.49-6699.8), respectively (Meizoso-Regueira et al., 2024). In China, approximately 3.12 million tons of sludge was disposed of as soil amendment, contributing at least 1013 MPs to agricultural soils annually (Li et al., 2022). Notably, atmospheric deposition, precipitation and irrigation may also continuously input MPs into the soil.
In conclusion, integrating the possibly underestimated MPs’ concentration, the fragmentation of large MPs, the heterogeneous distribution of soil MPs, the accumulation effects, and the projected increase in MPs contamination, we think 50 mg/kg is an appropriate concentration to represent real-world scenarios.
1.2 Regarding the proportion of MPs smaller than 5 μm.
Thank you for raising the question about the proportion of MPs < 5 μm in the total MPs (< 5 mm). Due to the limitations in the separation methods, MPs smaller than 5 μm are difficult to extract. As pointed out by Büks & Kaupenjohann (2020): “After density fractionation, the MPs are often separated from the dense solution by use of a fine-pored metal screen and cleaned by rinsing at the same place. To our knowledge, the smallest available mesh aperture is, to date, > 5 µm (optimized Dutch weave; GKD Group). Items with a profile smaller than this might become lost during the extraction. To date, we do not know anything about the contribution of this fraction exactly due to this filtration problem.” Furthermore, in the review by Kang et al. (2025), the authors conducted an analysis of 119 representative articles on soil MPs, stating that “However, current detection limitations hinder the accurate analysis of MPs smaller than 10 μm. Existing studies indicated that the smallest detectable MP sizes as 10 μm, 20 μm, 30 μm, and 50 μm, thereby neglecting the contribution of smaller MPs and nanoplastics to overall abundance.” To the best of our knowledge, to date, no available data exist on the abundance and mass concentrations of microplastics (MPs) smaller than 5 µm in real agricultural soils. Multiple studies suggest that the abundance of MPs increases as particle size decreases. For instance, Khan et al. (2023) reported that MPs ranging from 20 to 200 μm exhibited the highest abundance at 57.57% in agricultural soil. Li et al. (2025) analyzed the content of MPs (>20 μm) in long-term mulched soil and reported that the highest MPs content was found in the 20–50 μm (58.04 %), followed by 50–100 μm (29.16 %). However, these findings are constrained by the limitations of detection technology. We believe that the fragmentation of MPs in farmland will not stop at 20 µm, as larger MPs have been demonstrated to fragment into smaller MPs, and even nano-scale particles, due to prolonged exposure to physical, chemical, and biological factors. For instance, earthworms can ingest MPs from the soil and break them down into smaller particles during digestion (Boots et al., 2019). Additionally, 1 g of nylon can generate over 2×107 MPs of approximately 1 µm in size after 1000 hours of photo-aging (Pfohl et al., 2022). Agitation devices in wastewater treatment plants have also been shown to fragment MPs with initial sizes of 75, 150, and 300 µm into mean-sized NPs/MPs of 0.74, 1.14, and 1.88 µm, respectively (Pramanik et al., 2021). These 1 µm-scale MPs can subsequently become enriched in sludge-based fertilizers and may ultimately be introduced into agricultural soils.

Many foundational mechanistic studies in this field have employed similar or even higher concentration ranges. Our choice ensures that our results are directly comparable with the existing body of literature. For example, Li et al. Additionally, they performed soil culture experiments with the river sand and sandy soil samples amended with 0.2 μm PS beads at a target concentration of 150 mg/kg and 500 mg/kg, respectively. Jiang et al. (2022) explored the accumulation of nanoplastics by crops from soil amended with 50 and 250 mg/kg PS beads (80 nm). Sun et al. Similarly, many previous studies with focus on the effects of soil MPs have set the concentrations of MPs at 0.1% (i.e., 1000 mg/kg), 1% (i.e., 10000 mg/kg), and even higher. Research on pollutants must necessarily be based on levels in areas with relatively severe pollution (moderate or above) to be meaningful, as those are precisely the locations where the dangers occur. History shows that the severe lessons humanity has learned from pollutants are never determined by their average concentrations in nature. Taking soil Cd pollution as an example, a meta-analysis shows that the average Cd concentration in China’s arable soil is 0.27 mg/kg (Zhang et al., 2015), which is safe according to Chinese soil environmental quality for agricultural land (GB15618-2018). However, the Cd concentrations have a wide range from 0.01 to 152.95 mg/kg, with the standard deviation of 9.44 mg/kg (Zhang et al., 2015). When the pollution effects and risks of Cd in soil are studied, the pollution levels higher that 0.27 mg/kg must be considered. Theoretically, half of the concentrations may be higher than the average value (0.27 mg/kg). It is of great importance to include those scenarios with moderate and severe pollution levels due to their higher risks. In fact, a recent study (Hou et al. Global soil pollution by toxic metals threatens agriculture and human health. Science, 2025, 388(6744): 316-321.) systematically revealed that 14%–17% of global farmland is contaminated by toxic metals, directly impacting the health of 0.9–1.4 billion people, from which the Cd pollution rate in major rice-producing areas alone reaches 9%, posing great public health and ecological risks in many countries including China.

3. The fraction of MPs absorbed by plants
Another concern relates to the reported bioconcentration factor. For example, maize with mechanically damaged (deep-wounded) roots, the fraction absorbed has been estimated at approximately 1.7 × 10-6 (503/ 2.9×108 particles of PS-MPs 5 μm). This raises a question about the significance of such uptake in real field systems, especially considering the much lower concentrations typically present in soils (complex and heterogeneous both in terms of composition and pore structure) compared to the amounts applied here that used homogeneous potting mixtures. Again, please justify your approach.
Response:
(1) Thank you for your comments. Bioconcentration factor (BCF) is generally defined as the ratio of the concentration of a particular substance, such as a toxicant or an essential element, in the tissues of an organism to the concentration of that substance in the surrounding environment, such as soil or water. Our original description is “while in maize stems reached 503.4 ± 147.4 (1 μm) and 222.3 ± 63.8 (5 μm) items g−1.” Please note the unit for the MPs content we presented is items/g, while the unit in the soil is items/kg, so a multiplication by 1000 is required for the calculation. Thus, the ratio of 5 μm PS in maize stems and soil can be estimated by 222300 (particles kg-1) / 7.3×108 (particles kg−1), that is about 0.0003, which means about 0.03% of 5 μm PS was accumulated in maize stems. This is not surprising because, similar to other pollutants, MPs primarily accumulate in the root system and are difficult to transport to the above-ground parts, especially in soil. This study observed that the bioaccumulation of MPs from the environment in plants occurs primarily in the roots. For example, MPs content in the deep wound sites of taro roots was determined following a modified method based on previous studies 52,53(See the Methods section in the manuscript). As shown in Fig. 2g in the manuscript,the MPs uptake reached 695–719 mg/kg (fresh weight), which is more than 40 times that of the unwounded roots, and the BCF was calculated to reach 13.9–15.8. Furthermore, in actual field systems, crop root systems are more developed and transpiration is more vigorous compared to indoor cultivation, and roots may suffer multiple wounds throughout the growth stage, all of which could increase the root uptake of MPs. However, since the roots of most crops are not utilized as edible organs, we are more concerned with the MPs transferred to the edible parts. Finally, we would like to emphasize that given the enormous total amount of MPs in soil and their continuous aging/fragmentation/degradation, even if only 0.03% of these MPs are accumulated in the above-ground parts such as maize stems, it could pose significant health risks.
(2) This study found that wound-induced MPs accumulation in the edible parts can be as high as 161-503 items/g, which is equal to 1.61–5.03×105 items/kg. This value is hundreds to hundreds of thousands of times higher than the levels detected in various foods. According to Bai et al. (2022), the MPs contents in beverages, spices, honey, meat, vegetables, and tap water were reported as 0–5860, 2.00–1100, 0–698, 4.00–18.7, 900–3000, and 0–930 items/kg, respectively. Therefore, even in less contaminated farmland, if the uptake due to wounds is reduced to 1/10 or 1/100 of the value detected in our study, it could still lead to very serious food contamination, and the risk should not be overlooked.
(3) To address your concern regarding the significance of MPs uptake in the field, we conducted low-concentration (5 mg/kg) exposure experiments on taro plants in both laboratory and field settings (Fig. R1–R3). Specifically, under vermiculite culture conditions with the addition of 5 mg/kg PS-MPs, after 14 days of exposure, the MPs content detected in the corms was 39.1 ± 13.5 items/g (1 μm) and 50.9 ± 16.2 items/g (5 μm) (Fig. R1). Note that this accumulation corresponds to 24.3% and 37.5% of that under 50 mg/kg exposure (Fig. 3j in the manuscript), suggesting that at lower exposure concentrations, the MPs accumulation induced by wounding does not decrease proportionally with the environmental MPs concentration.
For the plants in the field, (Fig. R2 and R3), the specific method was as follows: with the plant as the center, a circle was drawn on the horizontal plane, and a sector area of 72° (72°/360° = 20%) was demarcated. At approximately 20 cm from the plant, the outer soil was excavated to cut off the roots within this sector, which was considered as 20% root wounded. Then, the area was backfilled with soil mixed with 5 mg/kg fragmented PVC-MPs (fluorescently labeled with Nile Red). After 14 days, the entire plant was excavated for subsequent microscopic and quantitative analysis. The results showed that under the 5 mg/kg exposure concentration, the MPs content in taro corms reached 105.6 ± 62.3 items/g. It is noteworthy that this uptake is close to the absorption amount obtained under 50 mg/kg exposure conditions (135.6–165.1 items/g in Fig. 3j of the manuscript). We believe this may be related to the following reasons:
a. Plants grown in the field are larger, with root diameter and xylem vessel diameter reaching approximately 2.8 mm and 107 μm, respectively, which are significantly higher than those under potted conditions (approximately 1.9 mm and 65 μm). This provides a more unimpeded pathway for the uptake and transport of MPs.
b. Field-grown plants can reach a height of 1 m, much taller than the 25–30 cm under potted conditions. In particular, their broader leaves provide a stronger transpirational pull compared to potted plants, promoting the movement of MPs in the vessels. Moreover, the number of roots per corm in field plants is more than twice that of potted corms, equivalent to providing more channels for MPs uptake.
c. The activity of soil organisms, especially microorganisms, may on one hand promote the movement of MPs, and on the other hand inhibit wound healing, thereby enhancing the absorption of MPs through wounds.

4. The severity and frequency of root wounding in field crops.
Finally, it is essential to address the occurrence of severe (deep) root wounding events in typical field-grown maize or other crops. Severe mechanical damage to roots, as simulated in some experimental studies, may not reflect the natural frequency of such events under standard agronomic conditions for the crops studied here. This strongly influences the likelihood of MPs entering plants in the field and should be carefully discussed when extrapolating greenhouse or pot experiments to real agricultural systems. Additionally, it is important to consider whether the common agricultural practice of using plastic mulch for maize and similar field crops should also be regarded as a significant concern.
Although we agree that deeply wounded roots can act as one of the major absorption pathways based on the study results, we remain deeply concerned about the generalization and applicability of these findings to real-world agricultural conditions.
Response:
4.1 The widespread damage to crop root systems in field conditions has been extensively documented in previous studies. The primary factors contributing to root damage include belowground pests, agricultural operations, and extreme weather fluctuations (such as freeze-thaw cycles, wet-dry alternations, and wind effects). Detailed explanations of these factors are provided below:
(1) Belowground herbivores pose a significant threat to global crop production. For instance, Zvereva and Kozlov (2012) found that on average, belowground herbivory led to a 36.3% loss of root biomass, which was accompanied by a reduction in aboveground growth (−16.3%), photosynthesis (−11.7%), and reproduction (−15.5%). Additionally, phytoparasitic nematodes are prevalent in a wide range of plants and crops worldwide, causing substantial economic losses (Mesa-Valle et al., 2020). According to the American Society of Phytopathology (APS), nematodes are estimated to account for 14% of global crop yield losses, equivalent to approximately $125 billion annually (Chitwood, 2003).
(2) Tillage activities frequently lead to root damage. We once conducted an investigation which showed that a single application of fertilizer in furrows resulted in a root breakage rate of 12.1% in maize plants (Fig. R4). Moreover, such top-dressing is applied 2 to 3 times during the entire growing season of maize in some regions of China. Additionally, it is noteworthy that “root pruning” is employed as a measure to increase crop yield in maize (Yan et al., 2022) and tuber crops (Gao et al., 2018). In these pruning practices, approximately one-fifth to one-third of the roots are severed to promote the growth of deep roots and improve water use efficiency (Yan et al., 2023).

(3) Extreme weather is another factor contributing to root breakage. As indicated by Gardiner et al. (2016), strong winds can cause root breakage and lodging, and most herbaceous crops can partially recover under sufficient water and nutrient supply. For instance, in the United States, lodging leads to a 5% loss in total maize yield annually (Duvick et al., 2025). In the United Kingdom, lodging affects about 16% of wheat and 35% of oilseed rape (Berry, P.M. and Spink, J.H., 2006).
(4) Thank you for your suggestion. We have provided a more detailed description of the prevalence of root damage in field crops in the Introduction section (Line 59-62).
"Root injury occurs commonly throughout plant life cycle20. During crop cultivation, practices such as inter-tillage, transplanting, root-pruning, weeding, and fertilization are effective for enhancing yield but also result in root trauma21-23. In addition, below-ground herbivores24 and extreme weather events25,26 can also inflict root damage." (Line 59-62)
4.2 In the discussion section, we have clarified the differences in root damage between field conditions and laboratory conditions. Furthermore, we have carefully discussed the situation in actual agricultural soil and added a description of the high risk of MPs contamination in soil and crops due to factors such as plastic film mulching to the discussion section (Line 323-337).
"It should be noted that the 20% root wound created in this study may not fully represent the extent of damage typically experienced by field crops under standard agronomic conditions. Furthermore, the quantitative analysis of MPs in the edible parts was conducted under pot-cultivated and well-watered conditions, and therefore may not be entirely representative of natural field environments. This is due to the fact that MPs mobility in agricultural soils is influenced by multiple factors, including MPs speciation, soil physicochemical properties, hydrological conditions, and biological activities—often exhibiting multifaceted dependencies without clear-cut trends associated with individual key parameters48. Specifically, factors such as higher clay content and water deficit may enhance MPs adsorption and sequestration, whereas high porosity, abundant soluble carbon, saturated field capacity, and increased transpiration driven by intense solar radiation may facilitate MPs mobilization49. Therefore, for farmlands with high MPs pollution, such as those with long-term continuous plastic film mulching and application of sludge-based fertilizers, customized field research tailored to specific crop types and cultivation practices is needed to accurately assess the risks of food MPs contamination induced by wound-entry." (Line 323-337)

(2) Regarding the entry of soil particles, previous studies have confirmed that components in soil, such as montmorillonite (Yang et al., 2025a) and kaolinite (Yang et al., 2024), can enter through cracks in the root and may be translocated to the aerial parts. Therefore, the possibility of soil particles entering roots with deep wounds cannot be ruled out. In fact, it is not only soil particles; microorganisms also tend to accumulate at the wound site and enter the root (Tsai, H.H. et al., 2025). However, these phenomena have been reported in previous studies and are not the primary focus of our current work. We are concerned that excessive discussion on the uptake of substances other than MPs through wounds might dilute the main theme of this manuscript, and we hope for your understanding regarding this point. We plan to conduct more targeted subsequent research to explore the specific mechanisms of whether MPs can interact with soil particles, microorganisms, or other pollutants and jointly enter the root system through wounds.
(3) Regarding comment on non-soil cultivation systems: To obtain complete root system architecture for better observation of MPs distribution in roots, the majority of existing studies on plant MPs uptake mechanisms have been conducted under hydroponic conditions (Table R3). Furthermore, hydroponic cultivation is widely used in research on the interaction mechanisms between plant roots and various environmental factors. For instance, a recent study (Tsai HH, et al. Localized glutamine leakage drives the spatial structure of root microbial colonization. Science, 2025, 390(6768):eadu4235) analyzed microbial colonization and aggregation mechanisms on roots, and their key findings were also derived from hydroponic experiments. The advantage of this approach lies in excluding the influence of uncontrollable variables, thereby ensuring clarity in mechanistic elucidation and reliability of experimental conclusions.
In this study, we adopted vermiculite cultivation for the following reasons: Firstly, it prevents uncontrollable and undetectable root damage, which could significantly interfere with the analysis of wound-mediated uptake mechanisms. In field soil, it is impossible to guarantee the extent of root wounding or to obtain plants with completely undamaged roots as controls, making the elucidation of specific wound-mediated uptake mechanisms unfeasible. Secondly, vermiculite provides adequate support for root growth, yielding a morphology similar to that of soil-grown roots while avoiding scratches from soil particles on the root surface. Thirdly, vermiculite exhibits excellent aeration, preventing hypoxia stress in roots and thereby eliminating interference from uncontrollable wounds caused by hypoxia-induced rot—particularly advantageous for long-term exposure experiments. Thus, our cultivation method offers substantial advantages over the hydroponic approaches used in prior studies. Additionally, we have further validated through soil cultivation experiments that wound-entry mode is universally prevalent.
(4) Regarding the novelty of this study. Thank you for pointing out the research by Li et al. (2020). Li et al. (2020) reported that submicron-sized (0.2 μm) MPs can be absorbed by lettuce and wheat through root cracks. In contrast, 2.0 μm PS microbeads could only penetrate the vascular bundle when secondary roots had just emerged through the primary root epidermis, and were first detected in the epidermis and vascular tissues of wheat after 48 hours. Notably, 2.0 μm PS microbeads were absent in the entire wheat root system lacking secondary roots. These findings were primarily confirmed through hydroponic experiments and further validated using river sand and sandy soil. However, the study provided only qualitative results based on fluorescent labeling and electron microscopy observations, without quantitative data.
Nevertheless, it is evident from their results that the penetration of micron-sized MPs through root cracks is minimal and slow. Our study reveals a more universal and rapid channel for micron-sized MPs to enter plants. The key innovation of our work lies in elucidating the wound-entry mechanism.
Therefore, our findings significantly differ from those of Li et al. (2020), with the main novelties as follows: (1) We are the first to demonstrate that deep root wounds serve as a critical pathway for MPs entry into plants, providing the most intuitive evidence (relevant descriptions have been included in the Abstract and Discussion sections); (2) We developed a novel method to supply quantitative data for the edible parts of crops; (3) We confirmed that 1 μm and 5 μm MPs can also enter the root system in large quantities, indicating that root damage substantially expands the size range of MPs absorption; (4) We utilized multiple crops, such as taro, corn, mung bean, and wheat, making the results more broadly applicable. (5) Additionally, based on our extensive research on various crops, crack entry may not be universally applicable to all plant species.
For instance, we observed that cracks in soybean roots can reach 40–50 μm, permitting the infiltration of 1 μm MPs (Fig. R6). Conversely, in taro, the lateral roots are so tightly fused with the main root that even 0.1 μm MPs cannot enter (Fig. R7). It is important to note that in soybeans, MPs entry is restricted to the crack areas and does not lead to penetration of the vascular tissues; thus, no subsequent translocation to the aerial parts was detected. As illustrated in Fig. R6, the vascular bundles of the main and lateral roots in soybean are interconnected and are continuously protected by the endodermis and vascular bundle sheath. We found no evidence of MPs directly penetrating these protective layers, and no fluorescent MPs were detected in the shoot vascular bundles. These findings suggest that the crack-entry mode is still species-specific and dependent on particular biological microstructures. In contrast, the wound-entry pathway established in our study appears to have wider applicability. However, these discussions extend beyond the scope and focus of our manuscript, and we prefer to avoid excessive evaluation of others' work within our text. We sincerely appreciate your understanding on this matter.
Finally, we would like to express our sincere gratitude once again for the thorough work and highly insightful comments you have dedicated to this manuscript. Your efforts have not only enhanced the quality of this study but have also inspired ideas for our future research.

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the comments regarding the title. After careful consideration, we believe that the original title was intended to highlight the core contribution of this study—revealing a previously underrecognized mechanism by which MPs are rapidly absorbed and translocated through wound pathways. Each word in the title was carefully chosen to accurately convey the central scientific findings of the paper.
In response to your concerns, key clarifications have been incorporated throughout the manuscript to prevent any potential misunderstandings among readers:
• In the Abstract, we explicitly stated the experimental conditions as "in both vermiculite and soil culture conditions."
• In the Introduction, we clearly described the cultivation setup: "The plants are cultivated in either vermiculite or soil substrates with root systems exposed to 50 mg kg−1 of diverse MPs."
• In the Discussion, we contextualized the conclusions by noting: "the quantitative analysis of MPs in the edible parts was conducted under pot-cultivated and well-watered conditions, and therefore may not be entirely representative of natural field environments."
Furthermore, we would like to note that most mechanistic studies to date—including those recommended by the reviewer in this and previous rounds of review—are also based on short-term container-based simulation experiments. For instance, Li et al. (2020) used hydroponic (beaker), sand substrate, or sandy soil culture in studies on wheat and lettuce. Taylor et al. (2020) cultivated Arabidopsis and wheat in sterile Petri dishes with 0.5% agar and 1/4-strength Hoagland medium. We believe that the current title effectively draws the attention of readers in related fields to this interesting mechanism, while the clear statements in the Abstract and main text ensure that the conclusions of our study are accurately understood.

The reviewer understands that transpiration can be high under field conditions. Both pot and field experiments can show high transpiration. Still, it should be noted that the reasons and contexts differ significantly: pots create an artificial stress environment, while fields reflect natural, often extreme, climatic conditions.
Response:
We understand the reviewer’s concern that pot experiments may overestimate crop uptake.
The innovation of this study lies in elucidating the mechanism by which root wounding affects MPs uptake. Therefore, we adopted a carefully controlled experimental protocol to minimize interference from numerous variables present in the field. Specifically, we cultivated different plant species in a consistent vermiculite/soil substrate, provided uniform nutrient supply, and sterilized the substrate to prevent the spread of wounding effects caused by microorganisms—thereby obtaining reliable mechanistic data under controlled conditions, which is essential for a mechanism-focused study.
We acknowledge the differences between pot and field conditions. Thus, multiple measures have been taken to simulate field conditions and enhance the representativeness of our results. First, a vermiculite and soil substrate closer to the field environment was used instead of the commonly employed hydroponic cultivation. Second, in addition to the focused study on taro and maize, we included mung bean and wheat to eliminate interference from crop-specific traits. Third, besides PS, we also examined MPs such as PLA, PMMA, PE, and PVC in the size range of 0.5–5 μm, covering various polymer types and particle sizes.
In fact, transpiration rates in field-grown plants are generally much higher than those in pot-grown plants. Taking maize as an example, data indicate that one acre of maize can transpire up to 4,000 gallons of water per day (Link 1 and Link 2). Based on typical planting density in farmland (approximately 10 plants/m²), this translates to a daily transpiration rate of about 350 mL per plant. In contrast, the daily transpiration of each maize plant grown in the greenhouse in this study was only 3.6 mL (see our response to the first round of reviewers’ comments). This indicates that even at a transpiration rate far lower than that of field-grown plants, sufficient transpirational pull can be generated to transport MPs from the root vessels to the above-ground parts.
The primary objective of this study is to utilize the controlled conditions of pot experiments to isolate and evaluate the specific role of root wounding—as a single factor—in the uptake of MPs by crops, thereby avoiding interference from complex field variables. We observed root wounding-mediated uptake of MPs across different plant species and growing media, suggesting that this mode of uptake has general relevance. As for the actual amount of MP absorption and translocation via root wounds in field-grown crops, it is inevitably influenced by factors such as MP type, crop species, growth stage, extent of injury, and various environmental conditions. We have explicitly addressed the limitations of extrapolating these results to field conditions in the Discussion section, and we believe readers will appreciate these points.

Root damage does not lead to the death of all functional cells, and damaged roots retain a certain capacity for water uptake. For example, during tree transplantation, although most of the root system is severed, the plant can still survive under adequate water supply conditions. However, damage to roots can compromise barrier structures such as the epidermis and Casparian strip, directly exposing contaminants to vascular cells and thereby facilitating their entry and translocation within the root system. Additionally, Figure 2c−f in our manuscript provides substantial evidence that MPs are transported through the vessels of injured roots, further indicating that damaged roots maintain certain water uptake and transport functions.
It is well known that plant vessels retain their water transport capacity after being severed, as evidenced by fresh-cut flowers: cut stems placed in a water-containing substrate can sustain the blooms and leaves for over a week. Moreover, plant wound healing typically requires several days or even longer, as previously reported (Wahrenburg et al., 2021; Iida et al., 2025), depending on various factors such as plant species, tissue type, developmental stage, and external environment.
